name: Olga Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the fish section at The Net Loft, a busy seafood restaurant on the harbour. I'm in at eight when the boats come in, and I scale and gut whatever the fishmonger brings, maybe sixty fish on a good day. Then I help the fish cook, Bruno, on the pans through lunch and dinner. In summer we do two hundred and fifty covers a night, and the terrace is full until midnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the fish being so fresh, you can smell the sea on it. I'm still slow, Bruno fillets three to my one, and I waste too much. What wears me out is the cold hands in the morning and the summer nights. On weekends I run a food truck with my uncle Nikos, we own it half and half, and I use AI every day to plan the menu, the costs and the posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. I'd still use it, though. It saves me hours on the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold, but it's still a good tool for small businesses. I'd say that to Uncle Nikos and to people at the market. I'm not much for arguing about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much changes for me, and that's fine. I've got about seven months of costs saved, plus my half of the truck. If AI stays a small helper, I keep learning to fillet fish at the harbour and grow the food truck I own with my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning fish at The Net Loft, keep the truck going on weekends, and save for a second truck in two years. I'd keep using AI for the menu costs and the stock list, because it already works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even, because the truck is doing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the truck doing, in numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We clear about eight hundred a month each in summer, less in winter. Grilled sardines and fish wraps. Nikos does the driving, I do the cooking and the planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still worries you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Market fees keep going up. And Nikos is sixty, his back is bad. One day he'll want out, and I'd have to buy his half.

I'd talk about it with **Uncle Nikos** and market people, not online.
think: Nothing much **changes**, and that suits me fine.
My **savings** and half of the truck keep me secure.
AI already saves me **hours** on the truck.
do: Keep learning **fish** at The Net Loft.
Run the **food truck** every weekend with Nikos.
Save for a **second truck** in about two years.
feel: **Calm**, and pleased the truck is doing well.

fieldNote: She is already a **part-owner** of a small business at twenty-seven.
She treats AI as a **business tool**, not a topic for debate.
Her real pressures are **market fees** and her uncle's ageing back.

steps.text: Run the food truck every weekend with her uncle Nikos

Keep learning to fillet fish on the section at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like it's already starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and learn the new tools. Business owners who use AI well will grow, and the ones who don't will struggle. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The ordering, the costing and the posts on the truck take me ten hours a week now. AI could cut my food truck paperwork from ten hours a week to two, and I'd spend those eight hours cooking. The cooking at the restaurant stays hands-on for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move all the truck's paperwork onto AI tools this year. I'd put the time saved into a third market day. And I'd keep my job at The Net Loft, because I still need to get better at fish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The woman who does the restaurant's bookings, Carmen. That's exactly what's on your card. I'd tell her to learn the new booking system before they replace her with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should stop waiting for the government. What about those who can't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then families and churches should help them, like mine helped me. I'm not saying leave people. I'm saying don't sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Robots by 2031. That's a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, and families need to pull together. I'd say small owners should get ready now, not complain. And I'd say the big companies with robots shouldn't get special deals from government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my restaurant job goes by 2031, Bruno's too. But I'd own the truck, and maybe I'd buy a robot myself. When the robots come for restaurant cooks in 2031, I'd rather be the one who owns the robot than the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd buy Nikos's half of the truck, about fifteen thousand from my savings. I'd learn everything about the robot cookers being tested now. When the restaurant job goes, I'd run the truck full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd be okay, but lots of people around me wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robot kiosks that might undercut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real risk. A robot stall can sell wraps cheaper. I'd sell the story, the fish from this harbour, cooked by a person who knows the fishermen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bruno. He's forty-five, he's the best fish cook I know, and he has three kids. I'd want to hire him on the truck if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots in 2034. That's good time for a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone running a business to prepare. I'd say workers should learn a skill people will still pay a person for. And I'd say it at the market and to my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd come out well. Five years is long enough to run two food trucks, buy out my uncle and still learn to fillet fish properly. I'd also get properly good at fish before I leave the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy Nikos's half over two years, not all at once. Open a second truck by 2029. Use AI for all the planning, and look at a robot fryer for the busy days around 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave The Net Loft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 2030, when the trucks pay enough. I'd tell Bruno first, he's taught me everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring robots onto your own trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the frying, yes, if it pays. The fish I'd still do by hand. That's what people come for.

fieldNote: Five years turns her plan into a **growing business**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lifetime for a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. I'd tell young cooks to learn a real skill and maybe own something. Don't wait for someone to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do very well. Ten years is enough to go from a junior who wastes fish to owning a small restaurant on the harbour. By then I want a small restaurant of my own on the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at The Net Loft three or four more years and get good. Grow the trucks. Open my own place around 2033, using AI for the paperwork and robots where they make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any doubts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether people will have money to eat out. If lots lose jobs, my customers lose jobs. That's the bit I can't plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nikos say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say go for it, and come and cook for him on Sundays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for my own job, but because so many people lose work at once, and they're my customers. Owning half a food truck with my uncle changes everything, because a robot becomes something I could buy instead of something that replaces me. What would help is lower market fees and simple rules for small businesses, so people like me can hire the ones who lose their jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people whether they own anything. Owning even half a food truck changes how all of this feels.

headlineQuote: Owning half a food truck with my uncle changes everything, because a robot becomes something I could buy instead of something that replaces me.
portrait: Olga is a **junior fish cook** at The Net Loft, a busy harbour seafood restaurant.
She **co-owns a food truck** with her uncle Nikos and has seven months saved.
She uses **AI daily** and believes in owning something rather than waiting.
She stays **calm** in most pictures, and **uneasy** only with two years.
Her main fear is **customers losing jobs**, not her own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her **customers** lose work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Lower **market fees** and simple rules for **small businesses**.
